q: Sound is a sequence of pressure waves which propagates through compressible media such as air or water.
e: True. Stiffer media generally carry the wave faster. Sound is a sequence of pressure waves in a compressible medium such as air or water. It is longitudinal, not a transverse electromagnetic wave.

q: Sound is a sequence of electromagnetic waves which propagates through compressible media such as air or water.
e: False. Sound is a sequence of pressure waves in a compressible medium, not electromagnetic waves. Light and radio are electromagnetic and can cross vacuum. Sound cannot.

q: During their propagation, waves can be reflected, refracted or attenuated by the medium.
e: True. Attenuation is the weakening, not amplification. While sound travels it can be reflected, refracted or attenuated by the medium. Polarization is not the usual sound story in this chapter.

q: During their propagation, waves can be reflected, refracted or amplified by the medium.
e: False. While sound travels it can be reflected, refracted, or attenuated, not amplified, by the medium. Viscosity and spreading weaken the wave. Amplification would require an active source of energy.

q: A relationship between density and pressure, affected by temperature, determines the speed of sound within the medium.
e: True. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum.

q: The viscosity of the medium determines the rate at which sound is attenuated.
e: True. In air and water that viscous loss is often negligible. Elasticity, not viscosity, is what sets the speed. Viscosity of the medium sets how fast sound is attenuated.

q: The viscosity of the medium determines the rate at which sound is amplified.
e: False. Viscosity sets how fast sound is attenuated, not amplified. In air and water that viscous loss is often negligible. The wave dies; it does not grow.

q: For many media, such as air or water, attenuation due to viscosity is negligible.
e: True. Attenuation is loss of wave amplitude along the path. Viscosity sets that damping rate for sound. In many everyday media the viscous loss is small.

q: For many media, such as air or water, attenuation due to viscosity is significant.
e: False. For air and water, viscous attenuation is usually negligible. Those media still carry sound well. Significant viscous damping belongs to much thicker fluids.

q: Speed of a sound wave can also be affected by the density, temperature, and elasticity of the medium through which the sound waves travel.
e: True. Different media therefore have different speeds. Frequency and amplitude are not the speed-setters here. Sound speed depends on density, temperature and elasticity of the medium.

q: Hence, the speed of sound will be different for different media.
e: True. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium.

q: Longitudinal sound waves travel faster in solids than they do in liquids than they do in gases.
e: True. Longitudinal sound is fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases. Stiffer coupling raises speed. The gas-first order is backwards.

q: Longitudinal sound waves travel faster in gases than they do in liquids than they do in solids.
e: False. Longitudinal sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. Stiffer, denser coupling in a solid raises the speed. The gas-first order is backwards.

q: Young's modulus and the bulk modulus are elasticity properties of the medium.
e: True. Integer path difference is bright; half-integer is dark. Young in 1801 showed the wave nature of light with two slits and measured wavelengths. The centre is bright because path difference is zero, m = 0.

q: Young's modulus and the bulk modulus are viscosity properties of the medium.
e: False. Young's modulus and bulk modulus are elasticity properties. Viscosity measures internal friction, which damps the wave. Elastic moduli set the speed.

q: The SI units of Young's modulus and the bulk modulus are $N m^{-2}$.
e: True. Integer path difference is bright; half-integer is dark. Young in 1801 showed the wave nature of light with two slits and measured wavelengths. SI units of Young s modulus and cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The SI units of Young's modulus and the bulk modulus are $kg m^{-3}$.
e: False. Young's modulus and bulk modulus have SI unit N m^-2, the pascal. kg m^-3 is density. Mixing those units swaps stiffness for mass per volume.

q: The level of intensity of a sound is measured relative to a reference intensity value $I_0$, taken as $10^{-12} W m^{-2}$ which correspond to the minimum intensity of sound that can be heard.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Stiffer media generally carry it faster.

q: The reference intensity value $I_0$ corresponds to the maximum intensity of sound that can be heard.
e: False. I_0 is the minimum audible intensity, the threshold of hearing, 10^-12 W m^-2. Maximum tolerable sound is a pain threshold, a much larger I. Level zero dB sits at that minimum, not at a maximum.

q: The decibel (dB) is the unit used for measuring sound intensity.
e: True. Each extra 10 dB is about ten times the loudness. Hertz is frequency; watt is power; dB is this logarithmic level. The decibel measures sound intensity level, 10 log10(I/I_0).

q: For every 10 dB added to the sound level, the loudness of the sound is increased by 10 times.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Loudness is the ear's sensation of a sound.

q: For every 10 dB added to the sound level, the loudness of the sound is increased by 2 times.
e: False. Each extra 10 dB multiplies loudness by about 10, not by 2. A jump of 20 dB is therefore about 100 times louder. The decibel scale is logarithmic in intensity.

q: Sound intensity is a direct measure of the power reaching an eardrum measured in $W m^{-2}$.
e: True. Force or energy without time and area are the wrong measures. Sound intensity is power per unit area at the eardrum, in W m^-2. The dB number is the level of that intensity, not the intensity unit itself.

q: Sound intensity is a direct measure of the power reaching an eardrum measured in dB.
e: False. Sound intensity is power per unit area at the eardrum, in W m^-2. The decibel is the logarithmic level of that intensity. Do not quote intensity itself in dB.

q: The threshold of hearing is also known as the minimum audible intensity.
e: True. It is a minimum, not a maximum or a pain limit. Levels in decibels compare I to that I_0. Threshold of hearing is the minimum audible intensity, I_0 = 10^-12 W m^-2, which is 0 dB.

q: Echoes are produced where a sound wave is reflected from a large and hard surface.
e: True. An echo is a repetition of the original sound. Soft rugs and carpets absorb instead of reflecting. Echoes come from reflection at a large hard surface.

q: Echoes are produced where a sound wave is reflected from a small and soft surface.
e: False. Echoes come from large, hard reflectors. Small soft surfaces swallow the wave. Padding and carpets are how you kill echo in a room.

q: An echo is repetition of sound due to the reflection of sound.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. An echo is a delayed repeat after reflection from a large hard surface.

q: An echo is repetition of sound due to the refraction of sound.
e: False. An echo is repetition by reflection, not refraction. Refraction bends the ray as speed changes. The repeat you hear is the bounce.

q: The echo or the reflected sound can be heard separately from the original sound if the source of the sound is much closer to the observer than to the reflecting surface.
e: True. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign.

q: The echo or the reflected sound can be heard separately from the original sound if the source of the sound is much further from the observer than to the reflecting surface.
e: False. You hear the echo as a separate sound when the source is much closer to you than to the reflecting surface, so the extra path is long enough. Far from you and near the wall, the delay collapses. Geometry of the bounce sets the gap.

q: Reflection of sound obeys the laws of reflection.
e: True. Hard walls keep those angles clean. Reflection of sound obeys the laws of reflection, same as light: angle in equals angle out. Refraction and diffraction are different bends.

q: To reduce the effect of echo in buildings, walls are covered up with padding and the floors are covered with rugs and carpets.
e: True. Soft padding absorbs instead of bouncing. Range follows from the go-and-return time, v = 2d/t. An echo is a delayed repeat after reflection from a large hard surface.

q: Echo can also be used to determine the distance d between a source of sound and the reflecting surface by using formula $v = 2d/t$.
e: True. Range follows from the go-and-return time, v = 2d/t. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it.

q: Some animals such as bats are known to use echolocation to navigate and locate their prey.
e: True. Bats navigate and hunt that way. Sonar is the engineered version in water. Echolocation means emitting sounds and reading the returning echoes.

q: Echolocation is the special ability of emitting sounds and interpreting the echoes.
e: True. Sonar is the engineered version in water. Echolocation means emitting sounds and reading the returning echoes. Bats navigate and hunt that way.

q: Echolocation is the special ability of absorbing sounds and interpreting the echoes.
e: False. Echolocation means emitting sounds and reading the echoes, not absorbing them. Bats and sonar both shout then listen. Absorption would erase the return.

q: A reverberation is a reflection of light or sound waves, or a wide reaching impact of an action.
e: True. It is not absorption, and it is not a single delayed echo you can count. Padding cuts reverberation by eating the bounces. Reverberation is a wash of many reflections, as sound bouncing around a large hall.

q: A reverberation is the absorption of light or sound waves, or a wide reaching impact of an action.
e: False. Reverberation is a wash of reflections, as in a large hall, not absorption. Absorption is how you reduce that wash. The wide-reaching-impact wording still points to a bounce, not a sink.

q: An example of a reverberation is the sound bouncing around in a large speaker.
e: True. It is not absorption, and it is not a single delayed echo you can count. Padding cuts reverberation by eating the bounces. Example of a reverberation is the sound cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Audibility means the ability to be heard or capability of detecting sounds in certain range of frequencies.
e: True. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Human audibility runs about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Below that is infrasound; above is ultrasound.

q: The range of frequencies a person can hear is known as the range of audibility.
e: True. Amplitude and loudness are separate ideas. Range of audibility is the frequency band a person can hear, about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound; above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 20 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: True. A different driver in place of humans would describe a different law. humans and normal have to stay with the same process.

q: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 200 Hz and the upper limit is about 20 000 Hz.
e: False. Normal human hearing starts near 20 Hz, not 200 Hz, and runs to about 20 000 Hz. 200 Hz is already a spoken-word pitch. The true lower limit is an order of magnitude deeper.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called infrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: True. Infrasound is sound below 20 Hz, inaudible as a tone, with long wavelengths that travel far. Ultrasound is the high-frequency opposite. Most echolocation and medical sonar are ultrasound, not infrasound.

q: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called ultrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: False. Sound under 20 Hz is infrasound. Ultrasound is the high-frequency side above about 20 000 Hz. Swap those names and medical imaging and earthquake rumbles trade places.

q: A vibrating ruler can be seen but not heard its vibrating sound.
e: True. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. Vibrating ruler can be seen but not cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: High frequency sounds which are above the upper limit of audibility (20 000 Hz) are called ultrasound which cannot be heard by human ear.
e: True. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging.

q: Bats and whales use ultrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use ultrasound.
e: True. Sonar is sound navigation and ranging: shout, time the echo, get distance. v = 2d/t is the go-and-return formula. Radar does the same job with radio waves.

q: Bats and whales use infrasound in echolocation and most sonar technologies use infrasound.
e: False. Bats, whales, and most sonar use ultrasound, whose short wavelength gives sharp echoes. Infrasound is the long-wave, low-frequency band. Navigation clicks are not infrasonic.

q: If you blow a dog whistle, a dog may bark in response, even though you do not hear any sound.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Blow a dog whistle a dog may cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Manufacturers of concrete use ultrasound to check for cracks or cavities.
e: True. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart.

q: A prenatal ultrasound test uses high-frequency sound waves, inaudible to the human ear, that are transmitted through the abdomen via a device called a transducer.
e: True. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging. Prenatal ultrasound test uses high frequency sound cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: With prenatal ultrasound, the echoes are recorded and transformed into video or photographic images of the baby.
e: True. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear.

q: Ultrasonic scalers use ultrasound to remove calculus (plaque) deposits from the teeth.
e: True. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Ultrasonic scalers use ultrasound to remove calculus cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The transmission of high energy ultrasound may result in the creation of cavitation bubbles.
e: True. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Transmission of high energy ultrasound may result cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Cavitation bubbles are created at sites of rarefaction.
e: True. A different driver in place of Cavitation would describe a different law. Cavitation and bubbles have to stay with the same process.

q: Cavitation bubbles are created at sites of compression.
e: False. Cavitation bubbles form at rarefaction, where pressure dips, not at compression. Ultrasound in liquid can open those voids. Compression is the high-pressure half of the cycle.

q: These cavitation bubbles may displace contaminant from surfaces.
e: True. A different driver in place of cavitation would describe a different law. cavitation and bubbles have to stay with the same process.

q: Ultrasonic cleaning is especially effective in the cleaning of irregular surfaces or internal cavities and passageways.
e: True. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature.

q: The sonar (sound navigation and ranging) is a type of technology that works based on echoes.
e: True. Radar does the same job with radio waves. Sonar is sound navigation and ranging: shout, time the echo, get distance. v = 2d/t is the go-and-return formula.

q: Infrasound waves have short wavelengths, and are thus unable to travel long distances.
e: False. Infrasound has long wavelengths and can travel long distances. Short wavelength belongs to ultrasound. Low frequency is why storms and explosions are heard far away as rumble.

q: Infrasound waves which have lower frequency and longer wavelengths are able to travel longer distances with less attenuation.
e: True. Most echolocation and medical sonar are ultrasound, not infrasound. Infrasound is sound below 20 Hz, inaudible as a tone, with long wavelengths that travel far. Ultrasound is the high-frequency opposite.

q: The Doppler effect or Doppler shift is the change in frequency of a wave related to an observer due to the relative motion between the source and observer.
e: True. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Usually, only the motion of the source and the observer directly towards or away from each other in the reference frame in which the wave medium is considered at rest.
e: True. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of frequency (pitch) heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: True. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of amplitude heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: False. The everyday Doppler example is a change of frequency, heard as pitch, as a horn approaches and recedes. Amplitude is loudness, not that sliding note. Approach raises pitch; recession lowers it.

q: There are three cases we encounter in Doppler effect.
e: True. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Three cases we encounter in Doppler effect cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: $f_o$ is frequency heard by the observer.
e: True. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed.

q: $f_s$ is frequency produced by the source.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it.

q: $v$ is speed of sound in the medium.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. V is speed of sound in the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves towards the source.
e: True. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: False. Plus v_o is for an observer moving toward the source, which raises the observed frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. The source signs are chosen the same way: approach up, recession down.

q: $-v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: True. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium.

q: $-v_s$ is used when the source moves towards the observer.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency.

q: $+v_s$ is used when the source moves away from the observer.
e: True. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency.

q: When observer and source are stationary, $v_o = v_s = 0$.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed. Away from the source you flip that observer sign.

q: The wavelength of light from a star observed from the earth shifts towards the red end of the spectrum when the earth and the star are moving away from each other.
e: True. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet.

q: The phenomenon of light shifting towards the red end of the spectrum is called blue shift.
e: False. Motion apart slides light to the red, longer wavelength, and that is red shift. Blue shift is approach, toward shorter wavelength. Stars receding from Earth are the red-shift case.

q: The velocity of the astronomical body moving away from the earth can be determined from the fractional change in wavelength.
e: True. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating.

q: If the star were approaching the earth the spectral lines would shift towards blue end.
e: True. star and approaching have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of star would describe a different law.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses electromagnetic waves instead of sound.
e: True. Bats navigate and hunt that way. Sonar is the engineered version in water. Radar is radio detection and ranging: electromagnetic echolocation.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses sound waves instead of electromagnetic waves.
e: False. Radar uses electromagnetic waves, not sound. Sonar is the sound version. The ranging idea is similar; the wave family is not.

q: The Doppler effect is used in some types of radar, to measure the velocity of detected objects.
e: True. A bat's hunt is sound, not radar. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Doppler ultrasound is a technique that is used to examine blood flow.
e: True. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Blood flow rates can be found by measuring Doppler shift in frequency of ultrasound reflected by red blood cell (known as angiodynography).
e: True. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging.

q: The pitch of the note (how high it is) is determined by its frequency.
e: True. Greater frequency, higher pitch. Amplitude sets loudness, not pitch. Pitch, how high the note is, is set by frequency.

q: The pitch of the note (how high it is) is determined by its amplitude.
e: False. Pitch is set by frequency, not amplitude. Larger amplitude makes a louder note. Higher frequency makes a higher note.

q: The greater the frequency, the higher is the pitch.
e: True. Pitch is how high the note sounds, and frequency sets it. Raise frequency and pitch rises. Amplitude changes loudness, not high-or-low character.

q: The loudness of the note depends upon the amplitude of the wave that produces it.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to A squared, and is the objective W m^-2 measure. Loudness itself is a subjective sensation. Loudness depends on amplitude: bigger A, more energy, louder note.

q: The greater the amplitude, the louder the note, because more energy is used to produce a larger amplitude.
e: True. greater and amplitude have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of greater would describe a different law.

q: The greater the amplitude, the softer the note, because less energy is used to produce a larger amplitude.
e: False. Larger amplitude means a louder note, because more energy went into the wave. Softer would be a smaller amplitude. Energy and loudness rise together with A.

q: Quality of a sound is the characteristic which distinguishes the two sounds of the same loudness and same pitch but emitted by two different instruments.
e: True. It usually grows with intensity, which itself grows with amplitude squared. Two listeners can disagree, so loudness is subjective. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium.

q: The notes produced by the violin is richer than others because it has more overtones.
e: True. A different driver in place of notes would describe a different law. notes and produced have to stay with the same process.

q: Notes of the same pitch played upon different musical instruments are distinguished from each other by their quality.
e: True. Amplitude changes loudness, not high-or-low character. Pitch is how high the note sounds, and frequency sets it. Raise frequency and pitch rises.

q: The timbre of a sound depends on its waveform, which varies with the number of overtones or harmonics.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Timbre, or quality, lets you tell instruments apart at the same pitch and loudness.

q: The intensity of the sound at a place is the energy transmitted per second per unit area held normally to direction of sound.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the amplitude of the wave.
e: False. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Double A and I becomes four times. That is why I carries A^2 in I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 A^2.

q: Loudness is a sensation and hence, unlike intensity, it depends on the observer.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Loudness is the ear's sensation of a sound. It usually grows with intensity, which itself grows with amplitude squared.

q: To the human ears, the loudness of the sound is subjective.
e: True. Two listeners can disagree, so loudness is subjective. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum.

q: To the human ears, the loudness of the sound is objective.
e: False. Loudness is a sensation, so to human ears it is subjective. Intensity is the objective watt-per-square-metre measure. Two listeners can disagree on loudness at the same intensity.

q: Normally the greater the intensity, the greater the loudness of the sound is.
e: True. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Sound intensity is power per unit area, in W m^-2.
